newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo changes stats methodology to reduce pensions.
newsitem.headline: Yugo changes stats methodology to reduce pensions.

text.p: Yugoslavia's Statitics Office has changed its method of calculating average monthly wages and pensions for 1997, leading economists to caution the decision was yet another attempt to postpone a radical pension reform.

Instead of calculating the average monthly salary based on the number of workers who received what they earned, the new methodology divides the sum earned by the total number of workers, including those not paid, the Statistics Office said.
Around 400,000 workers, or 20 percent of the workforce, did not receive January salaries because of lack of liquidity.
Since pensions are index-linked to wages, any movement in salaries is reflected in payments to the elderly.
After the January average wage showed a 12 percent fall against December, to 618 dinars ($112) from 702, local media said on Tuesday pensions will also be cut.

"This is only a cosmetic change. We persistently refuse to admit that our pension scheme does not work. But instead of reforming the system, we change statistics for the second time in the past three years," Stojan Stamenkovic, chief economist of the Institute of Economic Sciences, told Reuters.
Economists agreed oversized public spending had forced the government to make the change.
"The government lacks funds and this is the way to pay less to pensioners, who never receive in full what they are entitled to," an economist said.
To stifle widespread discontent among pensioners and workers, the government promised it would start paying pensions regularly in 1997 and promised higher living standards to all.
But instead of making progress, it already owes two months of outstanding pensions totalling around 2.4 billion dinars, economists said.
"Pensions will account for 20-21 percent of the total Yugoslav gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 estimated to reach 103 billion dinars," said Zoran Popov of the Economics Institute.
In 1995, pensions accounted for 13.8 percent of GDP and a year later grew to 15.8 percent of GDP.
"The situation is tragic because nobody tries to help out those unfortunate people," he said.
Popov cautioned there was no money left in state coffers and urged the government to reform the pension scheme.
Yugoslav pensioners receive up to 85 percent of the average monthly salary, depending on the nature of their retirement.

"The problem can be compared to two world oil shocks in the 1970s. Right now, the state must reallocate six to eight percent of GDP to meet its liabilities to a growing pensioner population. And the economy cannot sustain such reallocation any longer," Popov said.

The problem, partly seen as a consequence of demographic changes and a growing elderly population, became acute during the years of sanctions when the isolated economy had to provide money for all those who did not work.

To sustain current pension rights and pay out pensions which sometimes exceed average wages, Yugoslavia would have to more than double its workforce to 4.6 million workers out of a total population of around 10.5 million.

Economists do not see a quick remedy to the problem which will continue to burden the country's public spending planned to stand at some 47 percent of 1997 GDP, but they said the government needs to begin with a step-by-step reform.

Yugoslavia, still barred from international financial institutions, has an unofficially estimated $9 billion in external debt, another $4.5 billion owed to its citizens for old hard currency savings frozen in the early 1990s and already a $2.26 billion trade deficit.

"The state will have to tackle its external liabilities and in the meantime, people must get used to the state pension being a social minimum, while the rest will have to be provided through alternative pension schemes," Popov said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
